ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Ethical approval of the study was provided by the Institutional Research Board of the Charité -Universitätsmedizin Berlin.
We are grateful to the support staff and research assistants on the BPAPS project, and to all our participants, whose efforts make this research possible.
A total of n=46 participants were recruited (age range 12-31 years), with n=21 CHR-P individuals (mean age 16.8 ± 3.3 years, 17 females) and n=25 HCs (mean age 19.3 ± 5.6 years, 15 females).
All participants were recruited at the Department of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry, Charité -Universitätsmedizin Berlin, Germany.
Healthy control participants were recruited from the local community.
All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision and were not hearing impaired.
Only native German speaking, right-handed participants were included in the present analyses.
All participants provided written informed consent (when younger than 18 years, consent was also provided by a parent/guardian) and were paid 10 Euro per hour of participation.
During the Active listening block, participants were instructed to attentively listen to the story, while ignoring visual stimuli.

This was followed by a 20-item comprehension questionnaire, whereby participants were presented with statements about the story content and were asked to rate the validity of a statement on a scale from 0% to 100%, providing a measure of both comprehension accuracy and confidence.
Participants were seated in a sound-attenuated booth at 80 cm from the screen while EEG-data was collected using an actively shielded EEG-amplifier (ANT-neuro) and 64-channel Waveguard caps.
During the Passive and Passive-reversed blocks, participants were asked to perform the visual Flanker task.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p<0.05", Text = "For mean RTs, the interaction of Group and Speech Intelligibility was significant (LMM-ANOVA: F(1, 126)=6.45, p<0.05)."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report:
Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. live_data_statements: We are grateful to the support staff and research assistants on the BPAPS project, and to all our participants, whose efforts make this research possible.
A total of n=46 participants were recruited (age range 12-31 years), with n=21 CHR-P individuals (mean age 16.8 ± 3.3 years, 17 females) and n=25 HCs (mean age 19.3 ± 5.6 years, 15 females).
All participants were recruited at the Department of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry, Charité -Universitätsmedizin Berlin, Germany.
Healthy control participants were recruited from the local community.
All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision and were not hearing impaired.
Only native German speaking, right-handed participants were included in the present analyses.
All participants provided written informed consent (when younger than 18 years, consent was also provided by a parent/guardian) and were paid 10 Euro per hour of participation.
During the Active listening block, participants were instructed to attentively listen to the story, while ignoring visual stimuli.

This was followed by a 20-item comprehension questionnaire, whereby participants were presented with statements about the story content and were asked to rate the validity of a statement on a scale from 0% to 100%, providing a measure of both comprehension accuracy and confidence.
Participants were seated in a sound-attenuated booth at 80 cm from the screen while EEG-data was collected using an actively shielded EEG-amplifier (ANT-neuro) and 64-channel Waveguard caps.
During the Passive and Passive-reversed blocks, participants were asked to perform the visual Flanker task.

text.text: In the present study, we used electroencephalography (EEG) to investigate speech processing impairments in CHR-P. In a previous MEG study, we showed that speech entrainment in the auditory cortices was reduced in CHR-Ps and schizophrenia patients compared to controls (Grent-'t-Jong et al., 2024), with the most pronounced effect in the theta band (4.50-6.50 Hz).

text.text: However, the contribution of attention towards speech entrainment was not investigated.

To examine this question, we implemented a dual-task speech entrainment paradigm to separate the effects of bottom-up processing and top-down attention in CHR-P individuals and healthy controls (HCs).
We hypothesized that oscillations in the auditory cortices of CHR-Ps may be differently modulated when speech listening is task-relevant.
Specifically, we expected reduced speech entrainment in the delta and theta bands for CHR-Ps compared to HCs, consistent with proposed deficits in bottom-up speech processing in this population.

We also expected a difference in alpha entrainment, with CHR-Ps showing reduced alpha entrainment compared to HCs when the speech is not task relevant, indicating a group difference in attention-driven modulations of entrainment.
A total of n=46 participants were recruited (age range 12-31 years), with n=21 CHR-P individuals (mean age 16.8 ± 3.3 years, 17 females) and n=25 HCs (mean age 19.3 ± 5.6 years, 15 females).

text.text: All participants were recruited at the Department of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry, Charité -Universitätsmedizin Berlin, Germany.
Healthy control participants were recruited from the local community.
Ethical approval of the study was provided by the Institutional Research Board of the Charité -Universitätsmedizin Berlin.
All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision and were not hearing impaired.
Only native German speaking, right-handed participants were included in the present analyses.
All participants provided written informed consent (when younger than 18 years, consent was also provided by a parent/guardian) and were paid 10 Euro per hour of participation.
Participants listened to 5.8-minute children's Sherlock Holmes story (available online from OHRKA e.V.).
The story was presented in three listening conditions: (1) Active, (2) Passive, and (3) Passive-reversed (i.e., unintelligible time-reversed and noise-vocoded speech).
In all three conditions, visual stimuli corresponding to the Flanker task were presented at fixation while the story was played.
There was one block per condition.
During the Active listening block, participants were instructed to attentively listen to the story, while ignoring visual stimuli.

This was followed by a 20-item comprehension questionnaire, whereby participants were presented with statements about the story content and were asked to rate the validity of a statement on a scale from 0% to 100%, providing a measure of both comprehension accuracy and confidence.
Participants were seated in a sound-attenuated booth at 80 cm from the screen while EEG-data was collected using an actively shielded EEG-amplifier (ANT-neuro) and 64-channel Waveguard caps.
Reference and ground were placed on the earlobes and data were sampled at 500 Hz without online filtering (DC-250 Hz range).
The audio was presented through an EEG-compatible Etymotic Research (ER-3C) inner-earphone system at 50 dB above individually determined hearing threshold.

T1weighted structural magnetic resonance images (MRI) were obtained on a later date, with a 3T Siemens Prisma scanner using a 3D Magnetization Prepared Rapid Gradient Echo sequence (1x1x1 mm resolution, 176 volumes, TR=2500 ms, TE=2.64 ms, FA=8).
EEG data were pre-processed in MATLAB using the FieldTrip Toolbox (Oostenveld et al., 2011).

text.text: Alterations in language processing are a core symptom of schizophrenia, yet the relative contribution of bottom-up and top-down deficits remains unclear.
Here, we manipulated speechdirected attention to investigate how top-down processing impacts entrainment in the auditory cortex during language comprehension.

Our findings reveal that theta entrainment was reduced in CHR-Ps while delta and alpha entrainment were modulated by attention, suggesting a combination of both bottom-up and top-down mediated speech processing impairments in CHR-Ps.
In the current study, we observed increased delta entrainment for intelligible compared to unintelligible speech (Passive>Passive-reversed), demonstrating preferential entrainment for speech signals.

text.text: Moreover, we observe an effect of attention, whereby delta entrainment is further enhanced when attention is directed to speech (Active>Passive).

text.text: Thus, we demonstrate that speech entrainment in the delta band is sensitive to both bottom-up and top-down processes.
In CHR-Ps, theta entrainment was reduced across conditions, which is consistent with our previous MEG findings (Grent-'t-Jong et al., 2024).

text.text: Alpha entrainment showed a more complex picture.
When attention was directed away from speech, alpha entrainment was reduced in CHR-Ps but maintained in HCs.
Moreover, HCs showed longer RTs in the Flanker task when background speech was intelligible, potentially indicating distraction and interference by speech for HCs but not CHR-Ps.

Delta and theta oscillations are central to the bottom-up language processing and the encoding of speech information (Di Liberto et al., 2015; Giraud et al., 2007; Giroud et al., 2024; Meyer, 2018; Meyer et al., 2020; Peelle et al., 2013; Peelle & Davis, 2012).

text.text: Modulation of delta entrainment by attention is consistent with previous reports (Dai et al., 2022; Ding et al., 2018), and suggests that domain-general modulations of neural gain may enhance entrainment (Bouwer, 2022; Lage-Castellanos et al., 2023; Pesnot Lerousseau et al., 2021).

text.text: Furthermore, if entrainment emerges via stimulus-driven and linguistically-guided processes (Gwilliams, 2020; Meyer et al., 2020), then the observed theta entrainment deficit in CHR-Ps may contribute to disrupted bottom-up spectrotemporal and phonemic processing critical for speech encoding and subsequent linguistic processing (Giroud et al., 2024).

text.text: Alpha oscillations, which are proposed to reflect attentional control during speech processing (Wöstmann et al., 2017), are known to be disrupted in schizophrenia (Abeles & Gomez-Ramirez, 2014; Basar-Eroglu et al., 2008; Uhlhaas & Singer, 2015).

text.text: Reduced alpha entrainment was observed in the current study in CHR-Ps when attention was directed away from speech, while HCs showed elevated alpha entrainment irrespective of whether speech task-relevant or in the background.
There are two possible explanations for this reduced alpha entrainment.
First, modulations in alpha entrainment may reflect domain-general resource allocation.
If the CHR-P group have limited domain-general resources, this could lead to reductions in alpha entrainment to background speech when top-down attention is redirected away.
At the same time, even when speech listening is not the attended task, HCs may still have resources available to monitor background speech, resulting in elevated alpha entrainment.
Alternatively, it is possible that alpha entrainment reflects stimulus-driven exogenous attentional capture.

If CHR-Ps have deficits in bottom-up processing (perhaps due to dysfunctional theta oscillations) this could disrupt the stimulus-driven and linguistically-guided parsing mechanisms of speech entrainment, thereby disrupting the mapping between speech input and linguistic knowledge and preventing sufficient encoding required for exogenous (stimulus-driven) attentional capture.
In contrast, intact speech encoding and an intact mapping from speech to linguistic knowledge in HCs could give rise to exogenous attentional capture by speech and thereby enhanced alpha entrainment.
This explanation can account for both the attention-independent alpha entrainment and the distraction effect in the Flanker task in HCs.
It is also possible that both endogenous top-down control and exogenous stimulus-driven capture are both at work.

It is further supported by brainbehaviour correlations in CHR-Ps, in which greater alpha entrainment during Passive listening is associated with higher comprehension, while greater attention-driven delta modulations between the Active and Passive conditions are associated with fewer perceptual symptoms in CHR-Ps.
Our findings show that speech entrainment in CHR-Ps involves both bottom-up deficits in theta-band activity while delta-and alpha-band entrainment are impacted by attention.
Furthermore, CHR-Ps show less distraction and reduced alpha entrainment in the presence of off-task intelligible speech.
We postulate that reduced alpha entrainment is consistent with dysfunction in either exogenous attentional capture, top-down domain-general attentional control, or both, in this population.
Overall, our findings support disrupted entrainment as a potential locus of speech processing deficits in schizophrenia.

Future studies are needed to further characterize the contributions of stimulus-driven processing and linguistically-guided parsing to speech entrainment in general, particularly in the theta and alpha ranges, and to disentangle these factors in language processing in schizophrenia.

text.text: During the Passive and Passive-reversed blocks, participants were asked to perform the visual Flanker task.
The Flanker task included an array of 5 horizontally presented arrowheads, centred at fixation (extending approximately 10 degrees of visual angle).

The middle arrowhead was relevant for the task (press left or right button to indicate the direction of the arrowhead, 160 trials per run, 50% left button 50% right button response), and two flanking arrowheads were presented on either side of the stimulus.

The flankers were either pointing in the same direction (i.e., congruent, 50% of trials) or pointing in the opposite direction (i.e., incongruent, 50% of trials) with respect to the central arrowhead.

Confidence in story comprehension was positively associated with alpha entrainment during Passive listening, with higher confidence predicting greater alpha entrainment (BF10=5.263, Pearson's r=0.538).

In addition, scores on the SIPS/SOPS subscale of "perceptual abnormalities" (P4) were correlated with the difference in delta entrainment between the Active and Passive conditions (BF10=4.740, Pearson's r=-0.530).
